sections.section_title: Clinical Presentation and Diagnostic Dilemma in Early-Onset Hyperglycemia
sections.description: The clinical presentation of monogenic diabetes, specifically Hepatocyte Nuclear Factor 1-alpha (HNF1A) maturity-onset diabetes of the young (MODY), frequently mimics the phenotypes of both Type 1 and Type 2 diabetes, creating a significant diagnostic challenge for clinicians. In this case, a young adult male presented with marked hyperglycemia and glycosuria discovered incidentally during a routine health examination. Despite an HbA1c of 10.2% and fasting glucose of 12.4 mmol/L—levels often associated with severe insulin deficiency—the patient was notably free of diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA). sections.section_title: Pathophysiology of HNF1A-MODY and Mechanisms of Glycosuria
sections.description: The molecular basis of HNF1A-MODY lies in the disruption of a critical transcriptional regulator encoded by the *HNF1A* gene, located on the long arm of chromosome 12 (12q24). This gene spans approximately 24 kilobases across ten exons and encodes hepatocyte nuclear factor 1-alpha (HNF1α), a homeodomain-containing protein that functions as a dimeric transcription factor. HNF1α is ubiquitously expressed but plays a disproportionately vital role in tissues central to glucose homeostasis, specifically the pancreatic beta cells, liver, kidney, and intestine. In the context of this case, the patient's novel heterozygous mutation (p.N270S) resides within exon 4, which codes for the DNA-binding domain of the protein. sections.section_title: Diagnostic Reasoning: From Clinical Suspicion to Genetic Confirmation
sections.description: The diagnostic journey in this case illustrates the critical shift from phenotypic observation to genotypic confirmation required for identifying Maturity-Onset Diabetes of the Young (MODY). The initial clinical picture—a young adult with significant hyperglycemia (HbA1c 10.2%), glycosuria, and classic symptoms of polydipsia and weight loss—mimicked both Type 1 and Type 2 diabetes. However, specific features prompted a deviation from standard diagnostic pathways. The absence of acanthosis nigricans and a BMI of 24.6 kg/m² made severe insulin resistance less likely, while the strong multigenerational family history of early-onset diabetes suggested an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern rather than sporadic Type 1 or complex multifactorial Type 2 diabetes. sections.section_title: Precision Medicine Management Strategies for HNF1A-MODY
sections.description: The clinical course of this patient illustrates the critical transition from empirical diabetes management to genotype-guided precision medicine. Upon initial presentation, the patient exhibited severe hyperglycemia (HbA1c 10.2%) alongside classic symptoms of catabolism, including polydipsia, polyphagia, and weight loss. Despite a strong family history suggestive of monogenic diabetes, the immediate clinical priority was rapid glycemic stabilization to resolve glucotoxicity and prevent further metabolic decompensation.
